messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel was a 58-year-old widowed South Asian man who had spent most of his life working on the water, and he came to treatment after months in which an accident at sea had continued to intrude into ordinary moments with a force that left him unsettled and increasingly isolated. He described the event as a life-threatening accident that had happened while he was out fishing, when everything changed in an instant and he was left with the clear sense that he might not make it back. When he tried to tell it, he often stopped and shook his head, saying that he knew what happened but could not find the words to describe it properly. The account stayed fragmented in his telling, as if the experience itself remained too raw to be shaped into a story. Even now, when he tried to recall it, the memory did not feel settled in the past; it came back with the same terror he had felt then, as though he were once again in that immediate danger rather than remembering something finished.

In the weeks and months afterward, Ravi found himself reacting strongly to things that had never troubled him before. Conversations with strangers became uncomfortable, especially if someone approached him in a casual, friendly way and expected him to talk freely. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, and that first impression of unfamiliarity made him cautious and withdrawn. He also noticed a sharp reaction whenever people spoke about loss, particularly when a conversation turned to someone dying or a family being torn apart. Such talk seemed to open the door to the accident in a way he could not control, bringing back the same cold fear that had settled in his chest when he thought he might lose his own life. He was also affected by images of cars hit by accident, especially when he saw wrecked vehicles on the roadside or heard about collisions on the news; those scenes seemed to press against him with an immediacy that made it hard to look away, as though the sight might pull him back into the helplessness of the original event.

Ravi’s days became increasingly organized around a sense that danger could appear without warning. Unusual silence made him uneasy, and he said that when a room or house became too quiet he felt as if something dangerous was about to happen. This often left him on guard even inside his own home, where he should have felt at ease. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, turning his head at small sounds, checking what was happening around him before he could settle. Over time, this watchfulness became part of how he moved through familiar places, including his neighborhood and the areas where he worked. As a fisherman, he still had to be near boats, docks, and other busy waterside settings, but he now did so with a tension that made the ordinary sounds of the harbor feel loaded with possibility. He remained alert for anything that might go wrong, as if he needed to be ready for the next sudden event.

What troubled Ravi also changed the way he understood himself. He said that he no longer trusted his own body, because after the accident he had become painfully aware that it could fail him when he most needed it. That sense of bodily unreliability sat alongside a deeper uncertainty about who he was now. He felt he did not know himself anymore, and there was grief in the way he said it, as though the man he had been before the accident had not simply been shaken but was somehow no longer fully accessible to him. These thoughts made him quieter with other people and more hesitant in daily life. He was less willing to linger in conversation, less willing to let strangers draw him into talk, and more likely to keep to himself. The change was noticeable enough that it affected how he moved through his routines, and there were moments at work when he held back from exchanges that used to be easy for him.

By the time he sought help, Ravi had become worried by how often these reactions were appearing and how much space they were taking up in his life. He wanted relief from the sudden terror that returned when he thought about the accident, from the uneasy sense that silence meant something bad was near, and from the way everyday scenes could pull him back into that moment on the water. He did not describe himself as wanting to forget what happened so much as wanting to feel like himself again and to move through the world without constantly feeling as though danger were hiding just out of sight. What brought him to treatment was the fear that this was becoming the new shape of his life, and what he hoped for was a way to live without being pulled so vividly back into the accident every time something reminded him of it.
